prompt: What is an agribusiness opportunity?

options.text: A potentially profitable business idea within the agricultural sector, which may involve production, processing, distribution, marketing or service provision
A government grant available to registered farmers
A licence permitting the export of agricultural produce
A plot of land certified as suitable for farming

explanation: A potentially profitable idea inside agriculture, and the reach is wide: production, processing, distribution, marketing, or services.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition given in the unit and repeated in the in-text answer.
why.b: Wrong. Grants are not what the term means.
why.c: Wrong. An export licence is a compliance matter.
why.d: Wrong. Land suitability is a production input, not an opportunity.

prompt: An agribusiness opportunity is a potentially {{1}} business idea within the agricultural sector.
explanation: Profitable. The word is doing real work: an idea that cannot make money is not an opportunity in this course's sense.

prompt: According to the deck, an agribusiness opportunity requires which three things?

options.text: Market demand, scalability and compliance
Land, labour and capital
Seeds, fertiliser and machinery
Storage, packaging and branding

explanation: Demand, scalability, compliance. All three reappear as full criteria in the evaluation list.

why.a: Correct. The deck names market demand, scalability and compliance.
why.b: Wrong. Those are factors of production, not the requirements named.
why.c: Wrong. Those are input supply items.
why.d: Wrong. Those are value chain stages.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the six criteria for evaluating an agribusiness opportunity?

options.text: Market demand
Profit margin
Soil pH
Policy and regulatory compliance

explanation: The six are market demand, cost of inputs, profit margin, scalability, environmental and social impact, and policy and regulatory compliance. Soil pH is a cultivation requirement, not a business criterion.

why.a: Wrong as an answer. Market demand is the first criterion.
why.b: Wrong as an answer. Profit margin is the third criterion.
why.c: Correct. Soil pH belongs to Module Three, where oil palm needs 5.0 to 6.0.
why.d: Wrong as an answer. Policy and regulatory compliance is the sixth criterion.

prompt: There are {{1}} criteria for evaluating a successful agribusiness.
explanation: Six criteria. Nine is the number of value chain components, five the number of common problems, and four the number of trends, so Module Four has a count for every list.

prompt: How is market demand defined as an evaluation criterion?

options.text: The level of consumer interest and willingness to purchase agricultural products or services at a given price over a specific period
The total quantity of produce a farm can supply in a season
The number of competitors operating in a market
The price at which the government will buy surplus produce

explanation: Consumer interest and willingness to purchase, at a given price, over a specific period. The price and the period are both inside the definition.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition in the text and in the glossary.
why.b: Wrong. That is supply, not demand.
why.c: Wrong. Competition is part of market research, not this definition.
why.d: Wrong. No government purchase scheme appears in the course.

prompt: Market demand is the level of consumer interest and {{1}} to purchase agricultural products at a given price.
explanation: Willingness. Interest alone is not demand: it becomes demand when someone will pay.

prompt: Which of these does the text give as an example of an input cost?

options.text: Energy and fuel consumption
Consumer willingness to pay
The profit remaining after all expenses
The market reach of the enterprise

explanation: Energy and fuel. The full list is seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides, labour, machinery and equipment, transportation, and energy and fuel.

why.a: Correct. Energy and fuel consumption is on the list of input costs.
why.b: Wrong. That is market demand.
why.c: Wrong. That is profit margin.
why.d: Wrong. That is scalability.

prompt: Input costs have a significant impact on profitability, productivity and {{1}}.
explanation: Competitiveness. The same word runs through agribusiness innovation, which exists to improve efficiency and competitiveness.

prompt: How is profit margin defined?

options.text: The difference between production costs and sales revenue, that is the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all costs are deducted
The total revenue from all sales in a season
The cost of producing one unit of output
The share of the market a business controls

explanation: Revenue minus costs, expressed as a percentage of revenue. It is the criterion that shows whether the business is financially viable.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition in the text.
why.b: Wrong. Total revenue is only half of the calculation.
why.c: Wrong. That is cost per unit, which belongs to cost control in operations management.
why.d: Wrong. Market share is not defined anywhere in this course.

prompt: Profit margin is the difference between production costs and sales {{1}}.
explanation: Revenue. Input costs are singled out in the definition as the expenses that matter most to it.

prompt: What does scalability mean as an evaluation criterion?

options.text: The potential to grow in size, output, revenue or market reach without a proportional increase in costs or a drop in efficiency or quality
The ability to reduce output quickly when prices fall
The measurement of yield per hectare
The physical size of the farm in hectares

explanation: Growth without proportional cost increase. The phrase without a proportional increase in costs is the whole point: growing by simply spending more is not scaling.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition in the text and the glossary.
why.b: Wrong. Contraction is not what scalability describes.
why.c: Wrong. Yield measurement belongs to cost control and efficiency.
why.d: Wrong. Current size is not the same as the potential to grow.

prompt: Scalability is growth in size, output, revenue or market reach without a {{1}} increase in costs.
explanation: Proportional. The self-assessment comparison in Module One used the same idea: the agripreneur treats farming as a scalable business.

prompt: What does the criterion of environmental and social impact assess?

options.text: The sustainability of the business in terms of environmental stewardship and its contribution to the local community and society
The number of jobs the business can create in a year
The value of exports the business generates
The tax the business pays to local government

explanation: Environmental stewardship plus contribution to community and society. It is the criterion that stops the evaluation being purely financial.

why.a: Correct. This is the criterion as the text states it.
why.b: Wrong. Job creation is a benefit of agripreneurship, but not this definition.
why.c: Wrong. Export value is a market matter.
why.d: Wrong. Tax is not discussed in the course.

prompt: Policy and regulatory compliance covers laws and standards governing which areas?

options.text: Agricultural practices, trade, land use, labour, environment and public health
Only food safety and packaging
Only export documentation
Only land registration and taxation

explanation: Six areas, and the text adds a warning: compliance is not optional, it is a critical part of risk management, market access and business sustainability.

why.a: Correct. These six areas are named in the criterion.
why.b: Wrong, and the word only cuts the list to two of six.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute; trade is one area among six.
why.d: Wrong, and an absolute; land use is one area, taxation is not named at all.

prompt: Compliance is not {{1}}; it is a critical part of risk management, market access and business sustainability.
explanation: Not optional. The phrasing is unusually forceful for this text, which is what makes it examinable as wording.

prompt: How does Module Four define the agricultural value chain?

options.text: All processes, activities and stakeholders involved in producing, processing, marketing and delivering agricultural products from the farm to the final consumer
The list of prices at each stage between farmer and consumer
The physical transport route from farm to market
The sequence of crops grown on a field over several seasons

explanation: Processes, activities and stakeholders, farm to final consumer. Each step adds value, which is the point of the name.

why.a: Correct. This is the Module Four definition.
why.b: Wrong. Prices are one aspect of marketing.
why.c: Wrong. That is transportation and logistics, one component.
why.d: Wrong. That is crop rotation.

prompt: Each step in the agricultural value chain adds {{1}} to the product.
explanation: Value. The glossary puts it the same way: the full range of activities involved in moving a product from the farm to the consumer, adding value at each stage.

prompt: Which of these is one of the nine components of the agricultural value chain?

options.text: Support services
Agricultural tourism
Agricultural waste management
Agricultural policy and advocacy

explanation: Support services. The other three options come from Module One's twelve value chain segments, which is a different list from Module Four's nine components. Both are examinable, so keep them apart.

why.a: Correct. Support services is the ninth component in Module Four.
why.b: Wrong. Agricultural tourism is a Module One value chain segment.
why.c: Wrong. Agricultural waste management is a Module One segment.
why.d: Wrong. Agricultural policy and advocacy is a Module One segment.

prompt: Module Four gives {{1}} components of the agricultural value chain, from input supply to support services.
explanation: Nine. Module One listed twelve segments an agripreneur could venture into; Module Four gives nine components of the chain itself.

prompt: Which set gives the input supply stage of the value chain?

options.text: Seeds, fertilizers, machinery, agrochemicals and animal feed
Warehousing, cold storage and protective packaging
Sorting, grading, threshing and drying
Loans, insurance, extension services and ICT tools

explanation: Five inputs, supplied by agro-dealers, seed companies and equipment manufacturers. Each wrong option is a different component of the same chain.

why.a: Correct. These five make up input supply.
why.b: Wrong. Those are storage and packaging.
why.c: Wrong. Those are harvesting and primary processing.
why.d: Wrong. Those are support services.

prompt: Inputs are provided by agro-{{1}}, seed companies and equipment manufacturers.
explanation: Agro-dealers. They are the only stakeholder group named by title in the input supply component.

prompt: What does the production stage focus on?

options.text: Yields, quality and sustainability
Branding, pricing and advertising
Warehousing, cold storage and packaging
Loans, insurance and legal support

explanation: Yields, quality, sustainability. Production is crop cultivation or livestock rearing by farmers or producers.

why.a: Correct. These three are the focus of the production stage.
why.b: Wrong. Those belong to marketing and sales.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to storage and packaging.
why.d: Wrong. Those belong to support services.

prompt: Which activities make up harvesting and primary processing?

options.text: Sorting, grading, threshing, drying and slaughtering
Milling wheat into flour and turning milk into cheese
Branding, labelling and retailing
Loans, insurance and extension services

explanation: Five operations that add initial value and prepare the product for market. Milling wheat into flour and turning milk into cheese is secondary processing, and branding, labelling and retailing is tertiary value addition.

why.a: Correct. These five make up harvesting and primary processing.
why.b: Wrong. Those are secondary processing or value addition.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the tertiary form of value addition.
why.d: Wrong. Those are support services.

prompt: Harvesting and primary processing adds {{1}} value and prepares the product for the market.
explanation: Initial value. Primary form value addition in Unit 2 says the same thing: simple processes at the farm level, cleaning, sorting and grading.

prompt: What does storage and packaging achieve in the value chain?

options.text: It helps prevent post-harvest losses and improves shelf life
It raises the yield in the field
It replaces the need for transportation
It reduces the cost of seeds and fertiliser

explanation: Prevent post-harvest losses, improve shelf life. Post-harvest losses are also one of the five common problems, so the component exists to solve a named problem.

why.a: Correct. These two are the stated benefits.
why.b: Wrong. Yield is decided in production.
why.c: Wrong. Transportation and logistics is its own component.
why.d: Wrong. Input costs are a separate matter entirely.

prompt: Storage and packaging includes warehousing, {{1}} storage and protective packaging.
explanation: Cold storage. Inadequate cold chain facilities are named separately as a cause of post-harvest losses.

prompt: What does transportation and logistics cover?

options.text: Moving goods from farms to processors, markets or ports, including handling, distribution and logistics management
Only road haulage between farms
Only export shipping
The storage of goods in warehouses

explanation: Farms to processors, markets or ports. Ports are in the list, which is how export sits inside this component rather than outside it.

why.a: Correct. This is the component as the text describes it.
why.b: Wrong, and an absolute. Ports and processors are also destinations.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. Domestic movement is included.
why.d: Wrong. Storage is the previous component.

prompt: What is secondary processing or value addition in the value chain?

options.text: Converting raw products into finished goods, such as turning milk into cheese or maize into flour, which significantly increases market value and shelf life
Cleaning, sorting and grading at the farm gate
Branding and retail packaging of finished goods
Moving goods from the farm to the port

explanation: Raw to finished, with a significant increase in market value and shelf life. Milk into cheese is the example the course uses three separate times.

why.a: Correct. This is secondary processing or value addition.
why.b: Wrong. That is harvesting and primary processing.
why.c: Wrong. Branding and retail packaging is tertiary value addition.
why.d: Wrong. That is transportation and logistics.

prompt: Secondary processing significantly increases the market value and {{1}} life of the products.
explanation: Shelf life. The same argument appears in Module Two for processed fish and in Unit 2 for value addition generally.

prompt: What does marketing and sales involve in the value chain?

options.text: Wholesale, retail, online platforms and export markets, with branding, pricing and advertising strategies
Cleaning, sorting and grading
Warehousing and cold storage
Loans, insurance and legal support

explanation: Four channels and three strategies. The channels echo the four target markets from the fish marketing unit.

why.a: Correct. These channels and strategies make up marketing and sales.
why.b: Wrong. Those are primary processing.
why.c: Wrong. Those are storage and packaging.
why.d: Wrong. Those are support services.

prompt: What is the final stage of the agricultural value chain?

options.text: Retail and consumption, where consumers purchase and consume the product
Support services, which underpin every other stage
Marketing and sales, which generate the revenue
Transportation and logistics, which deliver the goods

explanation: Retail and consumption. Supermarkets, local markets, restaurants or direct-to-consumer sales are the places it happens.

why.a: Correct. The text calls retail and consumption the final stage.
why.b: Wrong. Support services are listed ninth but they run alongside rather than at the end.
why.c: Wrong. Marketing and sales precede purchase.
why.d: Wrong. Logistics delivers to the point of sale, not to consumption.

prompt: Which four things make up support services?

options.text: Financial services such as loans and insurance, extension services, ICT tools, and legal and regulatory support
Seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and machinery
Sorting, grading, drying and slaughtering
Branding, pricing, advertising and retailing

explanation: Finance, extension, ICT, legal. Poor extension services appear separately as one of the five common problems, so this component is where that gap is felt.

why.a: Correct. These four make up support services.
why.b: Wrong. Those are input supply.
why.c: Wrong. Those are harvesting and primary processing.
why.d: Wrong. Those are marketing and sales, and retail.

prompt: Support services include financial services, {{1}} services, ICT tools, and legal and regulatory support.
explanation: Extension services. Their inadequacy is one of the five common problems in agriculture, so the word appears twice in this unit.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five common problems in agriculture named on the deck?

options.text: Limited market access
Post-harvest losses
Overproduction of processed goods
Poor extension services

explanation: The five are limited market access, post-harvest losses, low productivity, input supply challenges and poor extension services. Overproduction appears nowhere.

why.a: Wrong as an answer. Limited market access is the first problem.
why.b: Wrong as an answer. Post-harvest losses is the second.
why.c: Correct. Overproduction is not among the problems; low productivity is.
why.d: Wrong as an answer. Poor extension services is the fifth.

prompt: The deck names {{1}} common problems in agriculture.
explanation: Five on the deck. The text then adds three more: climate variability, inadequate financing and credit access, and land tenure issues.

prompt: Why does limited market access reduce farmers' profit margins?

options.text: Because farmers have difficulty connecting directly with buyers or final consumers and must rely on middlemen
Because transport is too fast for perishable goods
Because government sets a maximum price
Because consumers prefer imported produce

explanation: Middlemen take a cut. Module One's answer to this problem was the mobile app that connects farmers directly with buyers, eliminating exploitative middlemen.

why.a: Correct. Reliance on middlemen reduces profit margins.
why.b: Wrong. Slow transport is the problem for perishables, not fast transport.
why.c: Wrong. No price control is discussed.
why.d: Wrong. Import preference is not named as a cause.

prompt: Farmers must often rely on {{1}}, which reduces their profit margins.
explanation: Middlemen. Selling to middlemen is also the traditional farmer's habit in the Module One comparison table.

prompt: Which three causes does the text give for post-harvest losses?

options.text: Poor storage and transportation infrastructure, inadequate cold chain facilities for perishables, and insufficient farmer knowledge of post-harvest handling
Pests, drought and flooding
High input costs, low yields and poor seed
Middlemen, price controls and export bans

explanation: Infrastructure, cold chain, knowledge. The in-text answer names the first of these as the major cause.

why.a: Correct. These three are the causes named.
why.b: Wrong. Those are climate and pest risks, listed elsewhere.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to low productivity and input supply challenges.
why.d: Wrong. Middlemen belong to limited market access; the other two are not in the course.

prompt: The major cause of post-harvest losses is poor storage and transportation {{1}}.
explanation: Infrastructure. The glossary defines it as the basic physical systems such as roads, power supply and logistics that support value addition and distribution.

prompt: What causes low productivity, according to the text?

options.text: Outdated farming methods and low mechanisation, poor quality seeds and lack of proper inputs, and limited knowledge of best agronomic practices
Excessive mechanisation and over-application of fertiliser
Too many extension officers per farmer
An oversupply of high-quality seed

explanation: Methods, inputs, knowledge. All three are the mirror image of what the agripreneur does differently in the Module One comparison.

why.a: Correct. These three causes are named for low productivity.
why.b: Wrong. Low mechanisation is the problem, not excess.
why.c: Wrong. The problem is a low farmer-to-extension worker ratio.
why.d: Wrong. Poor quality seed is the stated problem.

prompt: Input supply challenges are the high {{1}} and low availability of seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and machinery.
explanation: High cost, low availability. Cost of inputs is also one of the six evaluation criteria, so the problem has a direct effect on whether an opportunity is viable.

prompt: Which three symptoms does the text give for poor extension services?

options.text: Inadequate training and support from agricultural officers, limited use of technology in knowledge dissemination, and a low farmer-to-extension worker ratio
High cost of seed, low yields and poor storage
Middlemen, price volatility and export barriers
Climate variability, land tenure and credit access

explanation: Training, technology, ratio. The support services component of the value chain is where these should come from.

why.a: Correct. These three are the symptoms named.
why.b: Wrong. Those belong to input supply, low productivity and post-harvest losses.
why.c: Wrong. Middlemen belong to market access; the others are not named this way.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the three additional problems listed after the main five.

prompt: Beyond the main five, which three further problems does the text list?

options.text: Climate variability and environmental challenges, inadequate financing and credit access, and land tenure issues
Overproduction, price collapse and currency risk
Labour surplus, machinery surplus and input surplus
Pest resistance, soil salinity and water logging

explanation: Climate, finance, land tenure. All three appear again as challenges to value addition and innovation in Unit 2.

why.a: Correct. These three are the other problems the text names.
why.b: Wrong. None of these is listed.
why.c: Wrong. Shortage rather than surplus is the problem throughout.
why.d: Wrong. None of these is listed among the problems.

prompt: Land {{1}} issues are listed among the further problems facing agriculture.
explanation: Land tenure. It is the last of the eight problems and therefore the one most often left out of a list answer.

prompt: Which set gives the five market needs and trends the deck lists?

options.text: Organic foods demand, traceability systems, convenience foods, plant-based proteins, eco-friendly packaging
Precision agriculture, vertical farming, smart irrigation, data-driven farming
Limited market access, post-harvest losses, low productivity, input challenges, poor extension
Form, place, time, convenience, packaging and nutritional value

explanation: The five consumer-side market needs. The precision agriculture answer is the emerging technologies list, the limited market access answer is the problems list, and the form, place and time answer is the six types of value addition, so all four are real lists from this module.

why.a: Correct. These five are the market needs and trends on the deck.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the emerging technologies.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the five common problems.
why.d: Wrong. Those are the types of value addition in Unit 2.

prompt: The deck lists {{1}} market needs and trends in agriculture.
explanation: Five market needs, against four key trends. The two lists are adjacent and easily merged.

prompt: Which technology does the text name as an example of a food traceability system?

options.text: Blockchain
Hydroponics
Anaerobic digestion
Induced breeding

explanation: Blockchain. It is the only place the word appears in the whole course, which makes it a likely names question.

why.a: Correct. Blockchain is given as the traceability example.
why.b: Wrong. Hydroponics belongs to vertical farming.
why.c: Wrong. Anaerobic digestion converts POME into biogas.
why.d: Wrong. Induced breeding is an aquaculture technology.

prompt: Consumers want to know where their food comes from, which creates demand for food {{1}} systems, local sourcing and transparent supply chains.
explanation: Traceability. It is the first of the five market needs and the one with a named technology attached.

prompt: What is driving demand for sustainable packaging, and how are businesses responding?

options.text: Environmental concern over plastic use, met by adopting biodegradable packaging, reducing plastic use and exploring waste-reduction technologies
A shortage of cardboard, met by using more plastic
Government subsidy, met by importing packaging
Rising fuel costs, met by shipping in bulk

explanation: Plastic concern in, biodegradable packaging out. Eco-friendly packaging also appears in the fish marketing unit and again as packaging and branding value addition.

why.a: Correct. Environmental concern over plastic drives the three responses named.
why.b: Wrong. No cardboard shortage appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. No packaging subsidy is mentioned.
why.d: Wrong. Fuel cost is an input cost, not the driver here.

prompt: What three social changes have increased demand for processed, ready-to-eat and convenience foods?

options.text: Urbanisation, increasing working hours and busy lifestyles
Falling incomes, rural migration and smaller households
Improved cold chains, better roads and cheaper fuel
Government campaigns, school feeding and food aid

explanation: Urbanisation, working hours, busy lifestyles. The same demand drives convenience value addition in Unit 2, with its ready-to-eat meals and instant mixes.

why.a: Correct. These three are the drivers the text names.
why.b: Wrong. None of these appears in the passage.
why.c: Wrong. Those are infrastructure improvements, not demand drivers.
why.d: Wrong. None of these appears in the course.

prompt: Increasing global demand for organic, {{1}}-free products is pushing farmers towards organic farming.
explanation: Pesticide-free. Sustainable and organic farming is also one of the eleven aspects of agriculture from Module One.

prompt: Which growing market does the text name alongside plant-based proteins?

options.text: Dairy substitutes and meat alternatives
Fish meal and bone meal
Palm kernel cake and empty fruit bunches
Fortified flour and organic honey

explanation: Dairy substitutes and meat alternatives, creating opportunities for new agricultural products.

why.a: Correct. Both are named alongside plant-based proteins.
why.b: Wrong. Neither appears in the course.
why.c: Wrong. Those are oil palm by-products.
why.d: Wrong. Those are examples of product innovation and tertiary value addition.

prompt: Which set gives the four key trends in agriculture?

options.text: Precision agriculture, urban and vertical farming, water conservation and irrigation technology, and data-driven decision making
Traceability, sustainable packaging, convenience foods and organic products
Product, process, marketing and organisational innovation
Planning, organising, directing and controlling

explanation: Four technology-led trends. The traceability answer is the market needs, the product, process, marketing and organisational answer is the types of innovation, and planning, organising, directing and controlling is POCD, so all four sets of four in this module appear together.

why.a: Correct. These four are the key trends in agriculture.
why.b: Wrong. Those are market needs, which are consumer-led.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the four types of innovation from Unit 2.
why.d: Wrong. That is POCD, from Unit 3.

prompt: The text gives {{1}} key trends in agriculture.
explanation: Four trends against five market needs. Trends are technology-led; needs are consumer-led.

prompt: Which technologies does precision agriculture use?

options.text: GPS, IoT and data analytics
Hydroponics and aeroponics
Drip irrigation and rainwater harvesting
Anaerobic digesters and composting bays

explanation: GPS, IoT, data analytics. Each of the four trends has its own technology set, and mixing them up is the easiest way to lose the mark.

why.a: Correct. These three are named under precision agriculture.
why.b: Wrong. Those belong to vertical farming.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to water conservation and irrigation technology.
why.d: Wrong. Those are by-product management from Module Three.

prompt: Precision agriculture helps farmers make {{1}}-driven decisions, monitor soil health and improve productivity.
explanation: Data-driven. The in-text answer gives the reason for its popularity: it increases efficiency by reducing waste and improving productivity.

prompt: How does the text define vertical farming?

options.text: Growing crops in stacked layers, often indoors, using controlled-environment agriculture technologies such as hydroponics and aeroponics
Growing crops on terraced hillsides to prevent erosion
Growing trees and crops together on the same land
Growing crops under plastic tunnels in open fields

explanation: Stacked layers, indoors, controlled environment. Hydroponics and aeroponics are the two named technologies.

why.a: Correct. This is the definition given.
why.b: Wrong. Terracing is not discussed in the course.
why.c: Wrong. That is agroforestry, from Module One.
why.d: Wrong. Tunnels are not mentioned; the text specifies stacked layers indoors.

prompt: Vertical farming uses controlled-environment agriculture technologies such as hydroponics and {{1}}.
explanation: Aeroponics. Do not confuse it with aquaponics, which is the fish and plant system from Module Two.

prompt: Which technologies does the water conservation trend call for?

options.text: Drip irrigation systems, soil moisture sensors, and recycled and treated water use or rainwater harvesting
GPS-guided tractors and satellite imagery
Hydroponics and stacked growing layers
Anaerobic digesters and composting

explanation: Drip irrigation, moisture sensors, recycled water and rainwater harvesting. The driver is water scarcity worsened by climate change.

why.a: Correct. These are the water conservation technologies named.
why.b: Wrong. Those belong to precision agriculture and data-driven decisions.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to vertical farming.
why.d: Wrong. Those handle palm oil by-products.

prompt: For what three purposes are satellite imagery, sensor networks and AI models used?

options.text: Pest detection, yield forecasting and supply chain optimisation
Soil pH correction, irrigation scheduling and pruning
Branding, pricing and advertising
Sterilisation, threshing and pressing

explanation: Pests, yields, supply chain. The three cover the field, the season and the chain beyond the farm.

why.a: Correct. These three are the purposes named for data-driven decision making.
why.b: Wrong. Those are agronomic operations.
why.c: Wrong. Those belong to marketing and sales.
why.d: Wrong. Those are oil palm processing stages.

prompt: What four things must entrepreneurs do to thrive in the evolving agricultural landscape?

options.text: Recognise opportunities within the value chain, adapt to market demands, adopt new technologies, and implement sustainable practices
Buy more land, hire more labour, borrow more capital, and export more produce
Reduce output, raise prices, cut staff, and wait for subsidies
Specialise in one crop, sell to one buyer, avoid technology, and minimise record keeping

explanation: Opportunities, market demands, technology, sustainability. It is a summary of the whole unit in four verbs.

why.a: Correct. These four are named in the unit conclusion.
why.b: Wrong. Scaling by spending more is precisely what scalability is defined against.
why.c: Wrong. None of these appears in the course.
why.d: Wrong. Each is the opposite of what the course recommends.

prompt: Which two current trends does the self-assessment answer name as shaping the future of agriculture?

options.text: Digital agriculture, and sustainable climate-smart farming
Vertical farming, and rainwater harvesting
Contract farming, and farmer cooperatives
Traceability, and convenience foods

explanation: Digital agriculture with drones, sensors and analytics; and climate-smart farming such as agroforestry and organic farming.

why.a: Correct. These two are the trends named in the self-assessment answer.
why.b: Wrong. Both appear in the unit, but not as this answer's pair.
why.c: Wrong. Those are examples of organisational innovation in Unit 2.
why.d: Wrong. Those are market needs, not the trends named here.

prompt: Sustainable and climate-{{1}} farming adopts practices that reduce environmental impact, such as agroforestry and organic farming.
explanation: Climate-smart. Agroforestry is one of the eleven aspects of agriculture from Module One, so the course closes a loop here.

prompt: What solution does the self-assessment answer give for pest and disease infestation?

options.text: Integrated pest management, combining biological controls, resistant varieties and responsible pesticide use
Heavy application of broad-spectrum pesticide
Removal of all vegetation around the farm
Switching to a single resistant crop permanently

explanation: Integrated pest management, IPM. Three tools in combination rather than one applied heavily.

why.a: Correct. IPM combining biological controls, resistant varieties and responsible pesticide use.
why.b: Wrong. Responsible use is specified, not heavy use.
why.c: Wrong, and an absolute. Agroforestry deliberately keeps trees on the farm.
why.d: Wrong. Resistant varieties are one component of IPM, not a permanent monoculture.

prompt: How does the glossary define agribusiness?

options.text: The business sector encompassing farming and related activities including seed supply, agrochemicals, machinery, processing and marketing
The trading of agricultural commodities on an exchange
Farming carried out purely for family consumption
The regulation of agricultural markets by government

explanation: Farming plus everything around it: seed supply, agrochemicals, machinery, processing and marketing. It is the whole system, which is why operations management sits inside it.

why.a: Correct. This is the glossary entry for agribusiness.
why.b: Wrong. Commodity trading is not what the term covers here.

prompt: How does the glossary define the supply chain?

options.text: The entire process involved in handling, transporting and delivering agricultural products from farm to market or end user
The list of suppliers a farm buys inputs from
The sequence of crops planted over several seasons
The contracts between farmers and processors

explanation: Handling, transporting, delivering, farm to end user. It overlaps the value chain but is narrower: the value chain adds value, the supply chain moves goods.

prompt: How are post-harvest losses defined in the glossary?

options.text: The reduction in quantity or quality of agricultural products after harvesting, often due to poor storage or handling
Crops lost to pests before harvest
Produce that fails to sell at the expected price
The share of a harvest kept back for seed

explanation: Quantity or quality, after harvest, from poor storage or handling. Both halves matter: a crop that arrives spoiled has lost quality even if none of it is missing.

prompt: Match each evaluation criterion to what it measures.

pairs.right: Consumer interest and willingness to purchase at a given price
Expenses for the resources needed to produce agricultural goods
Revenue remaining after all costs are deducted
Growth without a proportional rise in cost or a drop in quality
Adherence to laws on practice, trade, land, labour and health

explanation: Five of the six criteria with their definitions. The missing one is environmental and social impact, which measures stewardship and contribution to the community.
